To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the ability to utilize organic forms of nitrogen is not a direct reflection of the ability of the fungal partner in isolation, and that colonization by mycorrhizae has no influence on the assimilatory pathways in the plant.

(1) mycorrhizas of Eucalypts can utilize organic N compounds as well as mineral N sources, and that the ability to utilize organic N compounds was not directly related with that of the fungal partner; (2) mycorrhization did not influence the pathway of N assimilation; (3) mycorrhiza‐induced changes in the host plant's physiology may be important for the utilization of organic N compounds.

mycorrhiza‐associated Eucalypt seedlings can assimilate a wider range of organic N compounds than uninfected plants, and that this ability is not directly related to the ability of the mycorrhiza fungus to assimilate N in pure culture.

mycorrhiza formation confers upon Eucalypt species the ability to assimilate organic forms of nitrogen that they cannot assimilate as seedlings.

, in Eucalypts, mycorrhiza formation is associated with the ability to utilize a range of organic N sources, but the ability to utilize these sources is not directly related to the ability of the fungus in isolation to utilize these sources.

the symbiotic association between Eucalypt species and Pisolithus sp., and between Eucalypts and Elaphomyces spp., confers on these plants the ability to assimilate a range of organic and mineral nitrogen sources.
